These contrasting findings warrant further investigation of what kind of morphophonological alternations hamper decomposition in spoken word recognition.

Although the cases of consonant mutation in Scottish Gaelic and vowel change in English show that decomposition remains operational in the face of some morphophonological alternations in the stem, the morphological boundary is still transparent in these cases. The case of Dabaw Bisaya opens the possibility that obscuring the boundary between two overt morphemes (i.e., prefix and stem) prevents decomposition. However, it is also possible that Pizarro-Guevara's study is underpowered, since they only included 15 experimental items in their substitution condition, resulting in 960 data points with 64 participants, far from the recommended 1600 data points (see Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018). The present study, therefore, revisits the question of whether obscuring the morphological boundary between two overt morphemes hampers auditory decomposition. Exploring this question is of prime importance as it will shed light on what factors trigger decomposition in spoken word recognition. In the present study, we address this problem using Tagalog, particularly looking at nasal assimilation and nasal substitution, which will be discussed in turn.

1.0.2 Why Tagalog?

In Tagalog (Austronesian, Philippines), affixing velar-final prefixes like /maŋ-, paŋ-, naŋ-/ to obstruent-initial stems can trigger one of two morphophonological alternations. First, the prefix-final velar nasal can take on the place of articulation of the initial sound of the stem, resulting in NASAL ASSIMILATION. For example, the velar nasal in maŋ-becomes mam-in mambúlag 'to blind (someone)'. NASAL ASSIMILATION is also triggered by liquid sonorants, surfacing as pan-/man-/nan-for l-and ɾ-initial stems. The phonological identity of the stem remains unchanged in NASAL ASSIMILATION, since there is no coalescence between the final velar sound in the prefix and the initial consonant in the stem (see Table 2A for examples).

Alternatively, the prefix-final velar nasal and the initial obstruent of the stem can coalesce resulting in a single nasal stop with the same place of articulation as the stem's original obstruent, resulting in NASAL SUBSTITUTION (Schacter & Otanes, 1972; Zuraw, 2010), like in Dabaw Bisaya. For example, the velar nasal in maŋ-and the initial consonant in túlak 'push' become one sound n in manúlak 'to push someone'. The phonological form of the prefix and the stem both change, and the morphological boundary between them is obscured at orthographic and phonological levels due to the coalescence of the prefix-final and the steminitial segments (See Table 2B for more examples). The Dabaw Bisaya results suggest that NASAL SUBSTITUTION poses a problem for decomposition into morphemes during spoken word recognition.

These prefixes have various derivational and inflectional purposes: maŋ-marks agent voice, naŋ-marks perfective aspect, and paŋ-typically creates reservational (e.g., /paŋ/+/ paléŋke/ 'market' becomes [pamaléŋke] 'for wearing at the market') and instrumental (e.g., /paŋ/+/púnas/ 'wipe' becomes [pamúnas] 'for use in wiping') adjectives (Schachter & Otanes, 1972). illustrate, when Tagalog listeners hear the phonological input mam, they could parse this as the maŋ-prefix after nasal assimilation (e.g., mam-búlag 'to blind' from /maŋ/+/ búlag/) or as the maŋ-prefix after nasal substitution (e.g., ma-mangká 'to ride a boat' from /maŋ/+/ baŋká/, which begins with the phonological sequence ma-) or even as the ma-prefixfoot_0 and the beginning of an m-initial stem (ma-múlat 'to open eyes'). This indeterminacy may lead the parser to either delay morphological decomposition, or to make errors. For example, mamangká and mamúlat could be erroneously parsed into /mam/+/angká/* and /mam/+/úlat/*, respectively, which are phonotactically illegal, since vowel-initial stems do not exist in Tagalog. However, the phonological sequence maN is followed by a consonant (/p, t, k, ʔ, b, d, g, m, n, ŋ, s, h, l, r, w, j/) in the case of nasal assimilation, while it is followed by a vowel (/a, e, i, o, u/) in the case of nasal substitution and when ma-is prefixed to a nasal initial stem. Perhaps, Tagalog listeners can exploit these phonological sequences as cues (i.e., maN+consonant or maN+vowel) to avoid misparsing during auditory word recognition.

Previous work has investigated whether nasal assimilation and nasal substitution hamper decomposition in visual word recognition. Specifically, Cayado et al. (2025) report behavioural masked priming and MEG evidence that skilled Tagalog readers decompose prefixed words that undergo nasal substitution and assimilation just as they decompose complex words with no alternation. However, Cayado et al.'s findings only address obscurity at the orthographic level (e.g., mang + bangka 'boat' = mamangka 'to ride a boat'), since they focused on visual word recognition. It, therefore, remains an empirical question whether variable morphophonological alternations negatively impact decomposition in spoken word recognition, where co-activated nasal-assimilated and nasal-substituted words may compete with each other and listeners are likely to make misparsings as the auditory information is processed incrementally.

As illustrated in Figure 1, nasal-assimilated and nasal-substituted cases, as well as ma-prefixed words attached to m-initial stems, are considered in parallel after hearing mam. It is only after hearing the consonant (i.e., the complex uniqueness point) that the correct parsing can be conducted.

Figure 1. Illustration of how a nasal-substituted word may be parsed despite co-activation and competition with nasal-assimilated words.

Using an auditory masked priming paradigm, the present study investigates [1] if obscured morphological identity in the prefix hampers auditory decomposition; [2] if obscured morphological boundaries hamper auditory decomposition; and [3] if variability in phonological patterns modulates auditory decomposition.

If decomposition is hampered by obscured morphological identity in the prefix, then reliable priming should only be obtained for prefixed words with no morphophonological alternation, while no such effects should be obtained for prefixed words with NASAL ASSIMILATION and NASAL SUBSTITUTION. In contrast, if decomposition remains operational despite obscured morphological identity, then reliable priming should be obtained for all 3 types of prefixed words. If an obscured morphological boundary between the /prefix/+/stem/ hampers decomposition, then reliable priming should only be obtained for prefixed words with either no morphophonological alternation or with NASAL ASSIMILATION, but not for prefixed words with NASAL SUBSTITUTION. However, if auditory decomposition is unaffected by obscured morphological boundaries, then reliable priming should be obtained for all 3 types of prefixed words. Finally, if variability in phonological patterns modulates decomposition, then larger priming effects should be obtained for nasal-substituted prefixed words with VOICELESS-INITIAL stems than VOICED-INITIAL stems, since nasal substitution is more likely to occur for voiceless-initial stems than voiced-initial stems. Similar priming should be obtained if phonological variability does not modulate decomposition in speech comprehension.

2.0 Materials and Methods

2.0.1 Participants

We recruited seventy-nine native speakers of Tagalog for the experiment via Prolific.co (mean age =36.58; Range = 18-59). Participants reported their city of origin in the Philippines. Only participants from cities where Tagalog is the dominant language were retained. Due to the multilingual nature of the Philippines, all participants also reported speaking English. Others additionally spoke another Philippine language (N=39), Spanish (N=4), Japanese (N=3), French (N=2), Mandarin Chinese (N=1), Thai (N=1), German (N=1), Italian (N=1), and Korean (N=1). All participants reported completing their primary and secondary education in the Philippines. The experiment was overseen by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board. All participants gave their informed consent and were remunerated £3.13 for the 30-minute experiment.

2.0.2 Design and Materials

We used an auditory masked morphological priming paradigm (Kouider and Dupoux 2005) with three critical conditions with 40 trials each: There were also two control conditions with 40 trials each (20 related, 20 unrelated):

IDENTITY condition, consisting of the same monomorphemic words for both primes and targets; and PHONOLOGICAL control condition, consisting of monomorphemic prime-target word pairs with phonological overlap in the second syllable, to replicate the phonological overlap in critical conditions. Figure 2A shows example trials for each condition. We included the IDENTITY condition to test the viability of auditory masked priming in Tagalog and in a fully online setting (all previous auditory masked priming experiments were conducted in a lab setting). Further, the PHONOLOGICAL condition was included to establish that the priming obtained in the critical conditions is not just due to the sounds they share but their morphological relationship. 6 practice trials were also added, consisting of 3 real words and 3 nonwords that were not used in the test phase.

The stimuli used in this study were the same as those used in Cayado et al. (2025), which were selected from a 198,303,250-word Tagalog corpus from SketchEngine (Kilgarriff, Rychly, Smrz, & Tugwell, 2004). Using the same Tagalog corpus, we created an IDENTITY condition, consisting of monomorphemic words. The targets in the NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, SUBSTITUTION, and PHONOLOGICAL conditions were list-wise matched for length (in syllables) and stem frequency. Related and Unrelated primes were pairwise matched for length (in syllables) and list-wise matched for lexical frequency. The same matching was employed in the IDENTITY condition. See Supplementary Material A on OSF for phonological and acoustic properties of the stimuli.

Nonwords were created using the Wuggy toolkit, which was enhanced with a Tagalog wordlist for training (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). The experiment included 200 nonword targets and 100 nonword primes as filler items. All nonwords were pronounceable and ranged from 5 to 10 letters in length to align with the critical and control items. To prevent participants from anticipating the lexical decision task, half of the nonword targets (100) were paired with real word primes that were 6 to 10 letters long. Both nonword and real word primes were matched by length across lists. In total, the experiment consisted of 406 trials.

All items, once selected, were subsequently recorded by a male native speaker of Tagalog. All items were recorded in a sound-attenuated Whisper Room booth at a sampling rate of 44,110 Hz. The native speaker read each item from a list in a relaxed yet careful manner.

Recordings were made while the speaker wore an omnidirectional head-mounted SM10A microphone made by Shure, which was connected via a Symetrix Audio 302 pre-amplifier to an Alesis Masterlink 9600. The speaker pronounced each item three times, and the best token of the three was selected for use in our experiment. 'Best token' was generally defined as the token with the clearest production, the most neutral intonation (i.e., standard declarative), and no non-linguistic intrusions (e.g., coughs). We demarcated, labelled, and extracted this token in Praat (Boersma & Weenink, 2011).

We followed Ussishkin et al. (2015 Ussishkin et al. ( , 2017) ) to create the stimuli. First, the prime-target pairs were matched with an auditory mask consisting of five unrelated Tagalog words with a very low phonological overlap with the prime and target. The words utilized as masks were recorded as part of the recording session described above. Second, all stimuli in the experiment-targets, primes, and masks-were scaled to match the global average RMS level across all recordings (approximately 82dB SPL) before being concatenated into stimuli. Third, primes and masks were durationally compressed to 35% of their original duration using the P(itch) S(ynchronous) O(ver)L(ap) A(dd) (PSOLA) algorithm, and their intensity downscaled to 15dB. This compression rate ensures that the prime is subliminally presented (see Kouider & Dupoux, 2005). Fourth, masks were temporally reversed. Finally, the components were concatenated into a single speech stream, such that a target (played at a normal speech rate and unattenuated) was superimposed on this stream, with its onset coinciding with the prime's offset, followed by four consecutive masks. A diagram illustrating the components of a typical trial (1 forward mask, 4 backward masks, prime and target) is shown in Figure 2B. The lists of prime-target pairs for each experiment can be found in on OSF: https://osf.io/4fgvb/overview?view_only=e822de4d87ed4041b525f1db76862774

2.0.3 Procedure

The experiment was administered on participants' computers using Gorilla (http://www.gorilla.sc/).

Participants were instructed to find a quiet area and sit in front of their computer wearing Before the experiment, participants were first given 6 practice trials to familiarize them with the slightly strange stimuli and task. They were told that "imagine you are at a party. There will be some noise from other people talking, but you will hear something that is louder than the noise. Listen for that thing and decide whether it is a word you know or not." The experimental items were then presented in two blocks, with 200 trials each. All participants heard the targets in both related and unrelated prime contexts. Targets were only heard once per block, and the blocks were interrupted by a short break to minimize long-lag priming effects. The order of items within a block was pseudo-randomized for each participant, and the order of the two blocks was counterbalanced across participants such that each block occurred as the first block for half of the participants. After the two experimental blocks, participants were asked to fill out a language questionnaire, and this completed the procedure.

2.0.4 Data pre-processing and analysis

All analyses were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2022). We first checked error rates on the responses to target words, and participants with an accuracy rate of <70% were excluded, which led to the removal of 10 participants or 12.65% of the data. Four participants were further removed as they reported another Philippine language as their native language (5.79%) in the language questionnaire. Sixty-five participants were retained for further analyses. Following Ussishkin et al. (2015 Ussishkin et al. ( , 2025)), reaction times (RTs) were measured from the target onset. For RT, trials faster than 300 ms were removed (0.05%), as well as trials that timed out (0.41%).

Following Baayen & Milin (2010) for further outlier trimming, we fit a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluded all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD (2.53%).

Finally, incorrect responses were excluded (2.53%). See Table 3 for by-subject mean RT and mean accuracy in each condition.

4.0 Discussion and conclusion

The main goals of the present study were three-fold: first, we tested whether obscuring the morphological identity of the prefix hampers decomposition; second, we examined whether obscuring the morphological boundary of a /prefix/+/stem/ hampers decomposition; and third, The majority of morphological processing studies have focused on written words, where all orthographic information is available simultaneously. Whether comparable decomposition processes operate during speech comprehension remains less well understood.

The present findings extend this literature across several dimensions: modality, by focusing on speech comprehension; typological breadth, by examining an understudied language such as Tagalog; ontological scope, by investigating underexplored morphophonological patterns; and methodology, by demonstrating that masked auditory priming can be conducted in a fully online setting. This methodological advance opens new possibilities for research by enabling access to more diverse participant populations and reducing the resource demands associated with lab-based experiments. Crucially, with respect to morphology, the priming effects observed here are consistent with the prediction that nasal-assimilated and nasal-substituted prefixed forms facilitate lexical access to their corresponding unchanged stems. This facilitation cannot be attributed to phonological overlap, as no priming was found for monomorphemic word pairs sharing the same second syllable, or semantic relatedness, given that masked priming effects have not been observed when masked at this compression rate.

Further, these priming effects emerged early during speech comprehension, since the primes were compressed to 35% of their original duration and only available for ~0.260 seconds (prime durations prior to compression averaged 0.745 seconds). The auditory masked priming effects observed in this study are consistent with what has been found in consonantal roots in Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015 (Ussishkin et al., , 2025) ) and Hebrew (e.g., Geary & Ussishkin, 2019), as well as initial consonant mutation in Scottish Gaelic (Ussishkin et al., 2017), but inconsistent with the lack of priming in word patterns in Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015 (Ussishkin et al., , 2025) ) and nasalsubstituted prefixed words in Dabaw Bisaya (Pizarro-Guevara, 2017). In Maltese, the absence of reliable priming is consistent with the proposal that the word pattern is a phonological element (see Fabri, 2009). In Dabaw Bisaya, Pizarro-Guevara's study is potentially underpowered, as discussed in the Introduction. Our results are aligned with models of speech comprehension that require or allow an initial decomposition stage (Balling & Baayen, 2012; Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994; Meunier & Segui, 1999; Schriefers et al., 1991; Taft et al., 1986; Wurm, 2000).

How, then, do listeners process and store words with morphophonological alternations?

In English, it has been observed that listeners can link stems with vowel change (e.g., sanity) to their unchanged forms (e.g., sane, sanely) in the mental lexicon (Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999).

In Scottish Gaelic, Ussishkin et al. (2017) revealed that native listeners were able to link the mutated (e.g., phòg 'kissed' with [f]) and unmutated forms (e.g., pòg 'kiss' with [p h ]) in the mental lexicon, and such linking happens early during processing as the primes were presented very quickly (i.e., compressed to 35% of their original duration), as in the current study. These studies provide evidence that decomposition remains robust in the face of morphophonological alternations, consistent with what has been found in the present study. However, the case of Tagalog is different: first, unlike Scottish Gaelic, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution are triggered by a linear prefixation process, where there are at least two overt morphemes; second, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution exhibit variability-it is not completely predictable whether nasal assimilation or nasal substitution will take place when velar-final prefixes are attached to obstruent-initial stems.

Therefore, results from our experiment shed light as to how native Tagalog listeners retrieve morphological pieces, especially when the prefix is phonologically obscured in the case of nasal assimilation and when both prefix and stem as well as their morphological boundary are phonologically obscured due to nasal substitution. We showed that hearing masked and compressed primes like mambúlag 'to blind (someone)' (from /maŋ-/+/búlag/) results in faster lexical decision to non-compressed targets like búlag, despite the nasalassimilated prefix form. Further, hearing masked and compressed nasal-substituted primes like mamitás 'to pick a flower' (from/maŋ-/+/pitás/) also resulted in faster lexical decision to noncompressed targets like pitás. Our results indicate that Tagalog listeners successfully decomposed masked and compressed primes into constituent morphemes, despite the fact that nasal assimilation obscures the phonological identity of the prefix and nasal substitution obscures the phonological identity of both the prefix and the stem, as well as their morphological boundary. In the case of nasal substitution, Tagalog listeners appear to be capable of linking the obscured form of the stem (e.g., mitas from mamitás) to its default form (e.g., pitás) at a very early stage of speech comprehension, consistent with what has been observed in Scottish Gaelic (Ussishkin et al., 2017). It is possible that listeners exploit the place of articulation in the surface coalesced nasal (i.e., m in mamitás) as a cue to recover the underlying obstruent of the stem (i.e., p in pitás). Finally, the way Tagalog listeners link these obscured stem forms to their unchanged stem forms are at a similar level of ease as linking two unchanged stem forms, as in the case of words that do not undergo any morphophonological alternations (e.g., maŋhúla 'to guess' linking to húla).

Unlike the case of Scottish Gaelic where initial consonant mutations are categorical, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution in Tagalog exhibit phonologically patterned variability. Specifically, when velar-final prefixes like /maŋ-/ are attached to obstruent-initial stems (e.g., p, t, s, k, b, d, g), it is not totally predictable whether assimilation or substitution will happen, but there are phonological trends-nasal substitution is more likely than nasal assimilation for voiceless-initial stems while the opposite holds for voiced-initial stems (Zuraw, 2010). We initially predicted that that such variability may result in occasional misparsing, thereby adding another level of processing difficulty when detecting the morphological boundary between prefix and stem. For example, when Tagalog listeners hear the input stream mam, the second nasal could belong to the prefix in assimilation (e.g., /maŋ-/+/búlag/ becomes mam-búlag 'to blind') or to the stem in substitution (e.g., /maŋ-/+/bangká/ becomes ma-mangka 'to go boating') or to the stem in ma-prefixed words attached to m-initial stems (e.g., ma-múlat 'to open eyes'). We hypothesized that the uncertainty that this induces may disrupt the retrieval of morphemes. However, we found that decomposition in auditory word recognition remains robust and operational in the face morphophonological variability, as evidenced by the similar magnitude of priming effects for ASSIMILATION and SUBSTITUTION conditions, and for both the VOICED and VOICELESS SUBSTITUTION sub-conditions.

It seems that native Tagalog listeners do not experience any difficulties with parsing such items. How, then, does decomposition happen during speech comprehension, particularly when the morphemes are obscured? A proposal by Cayado et al. (2025) for visual word recognition can also apply to spoken word recognition. Note that phonological sequences like maN, naN, and paN occur mostly in the context of prefixation. In a Tagalog corpus composed of books for elementary and high school students, the total token frequency of monomorphemic words starting with maN-/paN-/naN-phonological sequences is only 35.91 parts per million (ppm), while morphologically complex words with maN-, paN-, and naN-prefixes and the maprefix attached to nasal-initial stems have 8,369.88 ppm (see Supplementary Material B on OSF). Plausibly, Tagalog listeners exploit the phonological sequences maN-/paN-/naN-as a cue to initiate decomposition, since they most often signify that the word is prefixed. Further, these phonological sequences are followed by a consonant in nasal assimilation (e.g., mambúlag) and by a vowel in nasal substitution (e.g., mamangka) and in ma-prefixed words attached to nasal-initial stems (e.g., mamúlat). Perhaps, hearing the next segment (i.e., a consonant or a vowel) after maN-/paN-/naN disambiguates between nasal assimilation vs. nasal substitution or ma-prefixation, potentially avoiding any misparsing. The current data does not shed light as to how this disambiguation occurs. This hypothesis should therefore be tested in future studies along similar lines to Gwilliams & Marantz (2015)'s study on Arabic, with a single word reading study with concurrent MEG recording, in which the evoked MEG signal is modelled as a function of morpheme vs. phoneme derived surprisal measures. This would allow a direct investigation of how parsing of prefixed words unfolds over time and uncover what cues listeners use to trigger decomposition. Overall, the present findings indicate that auditory decomposition is equally rapid and easy for prefixed words without morphophonological alternation, with nasal assimilation, and with nasal substitution.

Previous models of morphological processing have not explicitly considered nasal assimilation and nasal substitution, but some may offer mechanistic accounts. In underspecification-based accounts, phonological changes are accommodated by allowing the phonological representation of morphemes to be underspecified with respect to those aspects of the input that change in certain morphological contexts (Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999; Reid & Marslen-Wilson, 2003). For example, the prefix /maŋ-/ and the stem /bangká/ 'boat' would be represented as [ma_]+[_angká] in the phonological lexicon, allowing for successful retrieval of each morpheme when they surface as full forms (e.g., maŋ-hula 'to guess', bangkáin 'use a boat') and as altered forms (e.g., mamangká 'to go boating'), since there will be no mismatch in the phonological representation and the segmented pieces at the surface level.

Alternatively, the readjustment-based account proposes that morphophonological operations are undone in the initial stage of processing while keeping the phonological representation of morphemes fully specified (Stockall & Gwilliams, forthcoming). Based on this proposal, the nasal substitution operation in mamangká ([/maŋ-/➔ [mam-]/_ [p, b]) would first be undone during decomposition, which would then allow the retrieval of the vocabulary items /maŋ-/+/bangká/. Perhaps, future auditory experiments can quantify the reliability of different morphophonological rules and examine how they affect decomposition, in order to tease apart which account is more plausible with respect to words that undergo morphophonological alternations.

To conclude, our results provide further evidence supporting the validity of the auditory masked priming paradigm in investigating morphological decomposition processes in speech comprehension (Kouider & Dupoux, 2005; Ussishkin et al., 2015 Ussishkin et al., , 2017 Ussishkin et al., , 2025;; Pizarro-Guevara, 2017). Building on earlier findings from auditory masked priming studies, we show that listeners successfully recognise morphemes within prefixed words despite morphophonological alternations that obscure the phonological identities of prefix and stem, as well as their morphological boundary. Further, listeners also successfully link the obscured form of the stem like in mamangká to their unchanged stem form like bangká, suggesting that these stems are linked together in the mental lexicon in such a way that speakers and listeners represent them as forms of the same stem. We also show that decomposition in speech comprehension occurs even when the listener has to deal with morphophonological variability that may cause uncertainty on where the morphological boundary is (e.g., /maŋ-/+/bangká/ becomes ma-mangka 'to go boating' vs. /maŋ-/+/búlag/ becomes mam-búlag 'to blind'). Taken together, these findings extend our theoretical understanding of how robust decomposition of a word into its constituent morphemes is in speech comprehension, and this contribution is only made possible by looking at an understudied language, Tagalog. We call for future research to look at other understudied languages with unique morphophonological operations in order to establish a more comprehensive understanding of morphological processing in different modalities.

Ethics and consent

The study was approved by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.

All participants provided informed consent prior to participation. All data were collected [1] NOCHANGE, consisting of prefixed words with no morphophonological alternations (maŋ-, paŋ-prefixes attached to h-initial, y-initial, and nasal-initial sounds); [2] ASSIMILATION, consisting of nasal-assimilated prefixed words; and [3] SUBSTITUTION, consisting of nasal-substituted prefixed words.

Within the SUBSTITUTION condition, we created two sub-conditions with 20 trials each: VOICED condition, which consisted of nasal-substituted prefixed words with voiced-initial stems (the less common pattern), and VOICELESS condition, which consisted of nasal-substituted prefixed words with voiceless-initial stems (the more common pattern). Across all conditions, the target words were each preceded by either a morphologically related prime or a morphologically unrelated prime (20 related, 20 unrelated). The prefixes maŋ-and paŋ-were used in all key conditions.

The models included CONDITION (NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, SUBSTITUTION, IDENTITY, PHONOLOGICAL) and PRIMETYPE (RELATED, UNRELATED) as fixed effects and their interaction.We also included other lexical properties, such as prime frequency (PRIMEFREQ) and target frequency (TARGETFREQ) as fixed effects. We set NOCHANGE and RELATED as reference levels for CONDITION and PRIMETYPE, respectively. To further test whether phonological variability affects decomposition, we also ran further analyses on the two sub-conditions within SUBSTITUTION: VOICELESS, with voiceless-initial stems, and VOICED, with voiced-initial stems.The fixed effects were STEMC (VOICELESS, VOICED) and PRIMETYPE (RELATED, UNRELATED), as well as their interaction. We used log-likelihood ratio tests using the anova() function to test for significance, comparing models with and without the interaction (CONDITION * PRIMETYPE vs. CONDITION + PRIMETYPE), and with and without the fixed effect of interest. Multiple comparison correction was performed using the emmeans package in R(Lenth et al., 2022) and alpha was .05. We tested for the inclusion of by-participant and by-target random slopes for CONDITION * PRIMETYPE interaction (Matuschek et al., 2017), but convergence issues emerged, prompting us to simplify our model. The final maximal model that converged included only random intercepts for Participant and Target: RT ~ CONDITION * PRIMETYPE + PRIMEFREQ + TARGETFREQ + (1|Participant) + (1|Target).

There was no significant main effect of CONDITION [X 2 (4) = 3.53, p = 0.472]. Planned pairwise comparisons of RELATED and UNRELATED RT means per condition using Tukey's HSD revealed significant priming effects for NOCHANGE [b = -22.96, SE = 6.57, z = -3.494, p = 0.0005], ASSIMILATION [b = -22.91, SE = 6.58, z = -3.480, p = 0.0005], SUBSTITUTION [b = -21.71, SE = 6.58, z = -3.302, p = 0.0010], and IDENTITY [b = -17.75, SE = 6.65, z = -2.670, p = 0.0076] conditions, while no priming effects were obtained for the PHONOLOGICAL condition [b = -0.43, SE = 6.72, z = -0.064, p = 0.9494].

exhibiting higher RTs than VOICELESS stems overall, and PRIMETYPE [X 2 (4) = 12.61, p = 0.0003], with UNRELATED primes exhibiting higher RTs than RELATED primes. Planned pairwise comparisons of RELATED and UNRELATED RT means per condition using Tukey's HSD revealed significant priming effects for both VOICED [b = -23.8, SE = 8.98, z = -2.653, p = 0.0080] and VOICELESS [b = -20.6, SE = 8.65, z = -2.381, p = 0.0173] conditions. The magnitude of priming effects between the two conditions was similar [b = -3.23, p = 0.796].

Figure 3.

Figure 3. The magnitude of priming effects was computed using the formula RT Related Prime -RT Unrelated Prime . (A) Priming effects in ms by condition, illustrating that all morphologically related prime-target pairs evoked priming, in contrast with phonological overlap prime-target pairs. (B) Priming effects in ms for Voiced and Voiceless sub-conditions within the Substitution condition. The points represent the means. The error bars represent the standard errors. The jitters represent individual datapoints.

[ 3 ]

we investigated whether variability in phonological patterns modulates decomposition. We found reliable priming effects in the IDENTITY condition while no such effects were found for the PHONCON condition, thereby supporting the validity of auditory masked priming in Tagalog and in a fully online setting. Further, reliable priming effects of similar magnitude were also observed in the NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions, suggesting that prefixed words were decomposed into morphemes during auditory word recognition, regardless of whether there is an obscurity in the prefix identity only (ASSIMILATION), or additional obscurity in the /prefix/+/stem/ boundary (SUBSTITUTION). Results from this experiment are consistent with the findings ofCayado et al. (2025), where prefixed words were decomposed into morphemes during visual word recognition, regardless of nasal assimilation or nasal substitution that visually obscured the morpheme boundary. Overall, the present findings and those ofCayado et al. (2025) unambiguously show that decomposition in both visual and auditory domains remains robust and operational in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure morphological identities and boundaries at the orthographic and phonological levels.
